title: New photos 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry hears
description: An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have execute
body: An inquiry into UK special forces operations in Afghanistan has released photos described as "essential evidence", showing soldiers could have executed unarmed people laying asleep.For the first time, the inquiry has made public photos taken of the deceased, across two SAS operations, that show multiple individuals lying in bed with shots to the head.The inquiry's lead barrister, Oliver Glasgow KC, said the photos may be evidence of possible war crimes and worthy of expert interrogation.The public inquiry is examining allegations that the SAS murdered unarmed civilians and detainees on night raids between 2010 and 2013 and planted weapons to cover up the killings.The graphic photographs show multiple unarmed people lying in bed. One person was tucked under a floral blanket, others with their heads on pillows, blood pooling around their heads. Blood spatter is visible low on the wall in one of the images, consistent with someone being shot while lying down.Glasgow described how many "look like they sustained head shots" and in a number of cases "there appears to be a dead body with his head on a pillow".He said further analysis may be able to confirm if the people in the photographs were "shot when asleep".Seventeen people were killed across the two operations which took place in Helmand province in 2011. The youngest of those killed in each of the operations were 15 and 14 years old respectively.Glasgow said the photos appeared to contradict the accounts given by the SAS and would have raised serious questions for the military police officers investigating the operations as potential murders.Lt Col John Harvey, who led the military police's murder probe, agreed they "didn't look right". He told the inquiry his team were clear the photos could be vital evidence.Despite the repeated requests of the police investigators to submit the photographs for further testing, this never took place.One of the investigators, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the BBC "you can see why we were concerned", adding: "Bullet marks on the walls so low to the ground appeared to undermine the special forces' version of events."The inquiry is subjecting the photographs to expert forensic analysis.BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed unarmed civilians and children for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.The photos appear to support the findings of Panorama's 2022 investigation into raids in Helmand province which took place a decade before.Panorama travelled to Afghanistan to gather evidence related to four raids on homes that killed 26 people.The BBC visited the same guesthouses where the photographs released by the inquiry on Tuesday were taken. Panorama's team were the first British investigators to visit the sites of the shootings, despite a five-year-long military police investigation.Official special forces accounts of the incidents claim Taliban insurgents opened fire on troops as they entered the compounds, forcing the SAS to return fire and kill those inside.However weaponry experts told the BBC evidence collected by Panorama indicated multiple rounds appeared to have been fired from above.This suggests those killed were either lying down or sitting against the wall and not in a firefight.Family members also told Panorama those killed had been shot cleanly in the head or chest - a common characteristic of a deliberate SAS shooting at close range.The photographs released by the inquiry show multiple "traumatic injuries to the head or face" of those killed by the SAS, according to its lead barrister.The inquiry also heard evidence that calls into question whether alleged war crimes were thoroughly investigated.  It heard how investigators were still in Afghanistan in July 2019 gathering evidence as senior officers prepared to close their murder investigation and inform ministers. The military police investigators were looking for eyewitnesses to unlawful killings and the planting of weapons.One member of the Afghan partner unit that served on operations alongside the SAS told military police he had personally witnessed a British soldier planting a rifle on an unarmed person after they had been killed.

schema.headline: New photos 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry hears

title: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction
description: Jonathan Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliam
body: Jonathan Ross is one of the country's best-known TV presenters, having regularly hosted celebrities on his Jonathan Ross Show, including David Walliams and Russell Brand.In the ITV documentary revealing the allegations, Ross is pictured at an event also attended by a woman who later made accusations about the conduct of Walliams.In his statement, Ross also addressed a joke he made at a comedy awards show in 2004, in which the punchline suggested Walliams would be "going home" with a 15-year-old.Ross acknowledged the controversial quip and described it as "tasteless".He added: "This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script writing team and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect."Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him."I also like to think that I would have acted upon that knowledge."Ross and Brand were also widely criticised for leaving lewd voicemails for Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs, the grandfather of Georgina Baillie with whom Brand was in a consensual relationship in the mid-2000s, during a BBC Radio 2 broadcast.Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years imprisonment for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and the Metropolitan Police has confirmed several people have approached them about the disgraced star since his conviction.If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction

title: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
description: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing cla
body: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

schema.headline: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT

title: Jensen Huang: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
description: Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.Jensen Hu
body: Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing. The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

schema.headline: Jensen Huang: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair

title: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
description: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a y
body: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be."You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited."Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one"."We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to quality for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it"."We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).This, the federation says, is "a low blow".Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000."Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls."Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits,  "getting them out their comfort zone"."If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"About 200km north, at  Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round,But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year."It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions."As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing."It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

schema.headline: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?

title: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident
description: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, on
body: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives."Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding."I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.But the workers have a huge task on their hands.Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely. But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary. However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers."Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall."For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean."We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

schema.headline: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident

title: More than 12 US military aircraft leave second UK base
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Military personnel are shown loading a US Air Force plane at RAF Mildenhall on Tuesday afternoonByCraig HoyleHarr
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Military personnel are shown loading a US Air Force plane at RAF Mildenhall on Tuesday afternoonByCraig HoyleHarriet Whitehead and Frank GardnerSecurity correspondentMore than 12 US Air Force aircraft have left a second airbase in Britain weeks after the US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford over a suspected Iran-linked security incident.The latest planes to leave, two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, flew from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk on Tuesday afternoon, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.The Wall Street Journal reported that this week's departures have been in response to a further threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified that claim.Downing Street has insisted British airbases are safe and that their security is a "top priority".Image caption, US military aircraft were pictured at Prestwick Airport, near GlasgowUsing public flight-tracking site Flightradar24 BBC Verify was able to see 10 USAF KC-135 tankers leaving RAF Mildenhall throughout Monday.Two aircraft which left the base on Monday initially flew to US bases in Germany and Italy.The first of these KC-135s flew to Spangdahlem airbase in south-west Germany where it completed a series of circuits before returning towards Mildenhall. However it did not land, instead circling back and flying in a holding pattern over Suffolk for nearly an hour before flying east and landing at Spangdahlem.The other aircraft was seen flying circuits over Aviano airbase in north-east Italy before going on to land at Spangdahlem. Neither aircraft was tracked landing back at Mildenhall.Later in the day more KC-135s flew from Mildenhall - two flew to Spangdahlem, one to the US base at Ramstein in Germany and four to Morón airbase in southern Spain. Three Osprey aircraft have have also left that RAF base. One aircraft, belonging to the Nebraska Air National Guard in the US, went to Prestwick Airport. It is unclear if this was a planned stopover before the jet returned to its home base.Asked about the flights, a Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC: "We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly ​according to operational ​requirements."Downing Street, meanwhile, has insisted that UK airbases are safe, with the prime minister's official spokesperson saying "the protection of our bases, both in the UK and across the world, is a top priority".Liberal Democrats defence spokesperson James MacCleary challenged this, writing on X that it "seems like every other day now the security of our airfields is either compromised or under threat".About 3,000 military personnel are stationed at RAF Mildenhall, which is around 80 miles (130km) north of London.There was no apparent additional security at the base on Tuesday, and the spaces from which the public could photograph aircraft remained open.The base is mostly used for refuelling and maintenance operations. Flights carrying US presidents, including Donald Trump, have often used it, and Trump came through RAF Mildenhall on his way back to the US from a Nato summit in Ankara in July.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US President Donald Trump at RAF Mildenhall in July after a Nato summit in TurkeyIt has also been used as a staging area for aircraft and material bound for the Middle East, with air refuelling tankers "forward deployed" to the region during operations against Iran.Asked about the US evacuating aircraft from RAF Mildenhall, Education Secretary Lucy Powell told BBC Breakfast she could not comment on ongoing operational matters.She added that "we take the security and safety of our bases incredibly seriously" and "we will always act on security intelligence when we need to".A US Air Force spokesperson said its aircraft "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements". "US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets," the spokesperson added.Former UK national security adviser Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We are talking about an airbase which houses these large tanker aircraft. Of course, they are large targets, an airbase has a long perimeter, so they are inevitably vulnerable."He added: "Nobody knows at this stage what this information was. I suspect part of it is an abundance of caution."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Aircraft left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and landed at other American bases in Europe and also at Prestwick Airport in AyrshireRetired Royal Air Force Air Marshal Greg Bagwell told BBC Verify "we need to keep an open mind" about the reasons behind the US aircraft movements.He suggested they could be the result of an exercise, or because the weather forecast meant it was safer to move the aircraft to other bases ahead of planned deployments elsewhere.Bagwell said the decision may also have been taken because of a hoax as part of "nuisance hybrid warfare" by countries like Iran - or it could be a genuine threat.He said the aircraft being dispersed to several bases could indicate the US was spreading them around to keep them safe and the moves have been "triggered by something".Bagwell added that the reason "we haven't seen an attack succeed or even happen" could be that "maybe our intelligence and our security is better than people might believe".Monday's departures from Mildenhall follow a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US-operated airbase in Gloucestershire.A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near that base in September. It later emerged that the US had pulled its bombers from there and returned them to America.Two British nationals appeared in court in October in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot.Seven men have been arrested as part of the investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing confirmed to the BBC on Tuesday, while an eighth has been interviewed under caution and since charged under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023.Iran has previously said that it considered UK bases used by the US for military strikes to be "legitimate targets".Additional reporting by Nick Johnson at RAF Mildenhall, and Rob Corp, BBC Verify.

schema.headline: More than 12 US military aircraft leave second UK base

title: Scotland vs North Macedonia: Scott McTominay reveals heart treatment at World Cup
description: Scott McTominay says he received treatment to correct an irregular heartbeat two days before Scotland's World Cup win over Haiti in June.The Napoli mi
body: Scott McTominay says he received treatment to correct an irregular heartbeat two days before Scotland's World Cup win over Haiti in June.The Napoli midfielder recently underwent an ablation procedure - a minimally invasive operation to correct irregular heart rhythms - in Manchester.At the World Cup, the 29-year-old was was put to sleep to correct his heartbeat and given the all-clear to play in the opening 1-0 victory over Haiti in Massachusetts. "I had to go and get the shock on my heart," revealed the former Manchester United player, who also played 90 minutes in the losses to Morocco and Brazil."It was two days before the Haiti game. You've prepared so well. I was in such good condition and then something like that happens. You're thinking, 'how is this happening to me?'"You have to get on with it, that's the cards that you're dealt in football. Sometimes, things don't go your way."I was 100% [fit], but obviously, whenever you're sat in a hospital bed two days before the first game of the World Cup about to get put to sleep, it's not ideal, is it?"

schema.headline: Scotland vs North Macedonia: Scott McTominay reveals heart treatment at World Cup

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. title: Why David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed
description: David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent inju
body: David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest. If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any wrong party seeks redress against journalists.After Walliams lost last week, and the court's judgment underlines how seriously it considered the risks to him to be, Mr Justice Nicklin asked whether there were plans for an appeal.But Walliams had not been able to give his lawyers instructions on how to proceed."There is a degree of urgency - the court has moved exceptionally quickly to accommodate this trial and produce this judgment," said Mr Justice Nicklin. "It is slightly concerning that there is not an ability to proceed today. I don't understand really. If I was satisfied that there were compelling reasons why permission to appeal should be granted I could say so now. "Sara Mansoori KC, Walliams' counsel, said the case raised "novel issues of law based on unusual facts" but because of the vulnerable nature of her client - in hospital - she needed more time.The judge gave Walliams until 16:30 GMT on Monday to come up with some proper grounds to challenge his decision. Those papers were never filed.The failure to launch an appeal bid meant that ITN and the Guardian were free to publish.While all this had been going on in court - there was a social media-sized elephant in the room. No end of people were posting 'It's David Walliams' and wondering why we bona fide journalists were not saying the same.When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication. That is why bona fide journalists who understand the law did not wade in.But there is a massive practical issue: how far does the writ of English law run in cyber space?One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west". That comment underlines the concern among legal professionals.But the question is how to enforce injunctions in an age of rapid fire digital gossip?If a newsroom were to breach an order, the nature of a large media organisation's audience means that publication would be seen by judges to be rather grave and the editor would likely be up in court.One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person by passing on gossip is obviously less impactful. If Chad from Utah reposts Dorothy from Liverpool's gossip, the chances of being hauled before a judge are even more remote.But what happens when thousands of people are all saying the same - and then their claims, perhaps based on a kernel of unreportable truth, are magnified by AI summaries and algorithms dripping content into phones?At that point, mathematically speaking the impact is greater than one single newsroom breaching an injunction.The public's perception of the Walliams case was complicated because his name became known from the start - but the furious gossip over who "PPT" really was shows there is an existential threat to how courts try to control information to prevent harm. And it's not clear whether they have any answer to it.

schema.headline: Why David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed

title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents. Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning. US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show. Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device. The BBC has contacted his representatives.Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court". He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician"."Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday. "We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor

title: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns
description: Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said.The Offi
body: Too many university students can use AI to complete assessments without staff finding out, the higher education regulator in England has said.The Office for Students (OfS) said "a significant proportion" of assessments are unsupervised and many can be completed to a high standard with AI, sometimes in minutes.It said this posed a "significant risk" to their credibility, and closed-book and practical exams were the most effective forms of assessments.Universities UK said many institutions had "made substantial changes" to make assessments "AI-proof".Universities that do not meet OfS quality standards could soon be banned from charging increased tuition fees or have caps imposed on their student numbers, under proposals that are now being consulted on.The new research from the OfS and Advance HE, a charity that gives awards for teaching excellence, is based on the views of 244 higher education staff and 91 students from at least 127 universities.It said "a significant proportion of assessments" were in "unsupervised, non-controlled formats where AI can be accessed by students completing them"."Many of these can be completed to a high standard using AI tools with limited engagement from students," it added.It also concluded it was "frequently possible" for students to use AI "in ways that cannot be reliably detected".Unsupervised assessment can include coursework, but also remote online exams. They were rolled out widely during Covid, and research from Swansea University, external last year suggests 93 universities in the UK still use them in some form.Josh Fleming, director of strategy and delivery at the OfS, said there were "fantastic" examples of universities seizing opportunities presented by AI, but there should be "far greater use of AI-free assessment"."It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them," he said.Kathryn Harrison-Graves, deputy chief executive at Advance HE, said students wanted "greater clarity about what is expected of them" but staff had "varying levels of confidence and support".The OfS said it had heard of cases where students were completing entire assessments within minutes using AI and receiving similar grades to those who had not.Some staff, meanwhile, were receiving lots of assignments that looked the same, and did not think their institution's assessments were "fit for purpose".Other staff described a "polarised atmosphere" between students who used AI and other "conscientious objectors" who avoided it on environmental and other grounds.The research said AI literacy for students was important during and after university, and some institutions were clearly communicating to students where AI can and cannot be used in assessments.But it said there was "an urgent need" to ensure that remote or "non-secure" assessments "maintain their validity despite the availability of AI tools, meaning they effectively assess the knowledge and skills they are designed to measure"."If it becomes possible to complete an assessment using AI without the knowledge and skills being tested, the assessment should be replaced," it added.Universities UK, which represents more than 140 institutions, said universities were "making significant progress" adapting to AI."There is further to go but many have made substantial changes to how they assess students. This includes more in-person exams, presentations, vivas, process-based assessment and assessments that integrate AI in a controlled way," a spokesperson said."Different subjects will require different approaches, and universities should have the flexibility to adopt assessment methods that best support learning outcomes."Lewis Wilson, from the National Union of Students, said AI was threatening "traditional" ways of learning that students and staff "have long said is not fit for purpose" - including essay questions, handouts and slideshows."It's time to get rid of the outdated methods, that have been kept around in the name of tradition, and instead encourage the innovative practice we see across the sector, co-designed with students based on what they want from higher education," he said.

schema.headline: Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns

title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
description: An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol
body: An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill. A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now. In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday. His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote. The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January. President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED"."Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS. "My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year. The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail. In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval. The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific  Ocean and Caribbean Sea. At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated". Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations". "This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said. He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February. He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

schema.headline: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now

title: Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP
description: The next census should include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English, according to a group of
body: The next census should include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as black English or Asian English, according to a group of MPs.Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde told the BBC that "most people" in the country believe "you don't have to be white to be English", as he called for the categories to be updated in a similar way to changes in Wales and Scotland.At the 2021 census, the ethnic group section saw English offered only within the white category.Babarinde's proposal, dubbed the "St George's Bill", aims to broaden the options and its supporters include Labour's David Lammy and Conservative Sir James Cleverly. It was tabled in the House of Commons on Tuesday.In his speech to introduce his private member's bill (PMB), Babarinde told MPs he is a "proud Englishman" and has "proud Nigerian heritage".He said: "But my parents and I were born in England, we grew up in England, our home is in England, yet some voices attempt to reduce Englishness to a skin colour and to a bloodline."Well, if we're going to go down that path, my mum's side of the family has been English for as far back as we have traced."The Eastbourne MP said he had received "death threats for daring to say that you don't have to be white to be English".He added "English ethnicity is real" before arguing it is a "matter of historical fact that it has never been one bloodline" and "even our Royal Family has German roots". "Is the King not English either, I ask."Addressing the ethnicity section of the census, Babarinde said the "only box that says English sits under the white category".He added: "If you are black, the form offers you black British, if you are Asian, it offers you Asian British, but not English."Now, the same question in the Welsh census offers a black Welsh category. In Scotland, the census offers Scottish Asian, for example."Yet the best that England offers in our census is a miscellaneous write-in box that may as well be the margin."Lammy, a former deputy prime minister, said in a statement: "It is quite absurd that neither I or my mixed heritage children can describe themselves as black or mixed race and English on our census form."I have long campaigned for us to change to the position enjoyed by others in Wales and Scotland.  We have to end this backward racial gatekeeping."Babarinde told the BBC he had brought forward the PMB because there were "some corners of our politics who are attempting to gatekeep Englishness for people who are a particular colour".He also said there are "people like Suella Braverman who have really undermined and questioned the Englishness of people like me".In 2025, Braverman - then a Conservative MP before her defection to Reform UK - wrote in the Daily Telegraph, external that she was British Asian but said she "cannot claim to be English" despite being born and educated in England.In recent weeks, Braverman has reaffirmed her position and wrote on X, external: "To say I'm English is to take a 'laissez-faire, anything-goes' attitude to ethnicity, citizenship and identity. It also denies me my Asian heritage."She also said "Englishness is an ethnicity", adding: "There have been English people for centuries and we need to recognise this more if we are to start taking a more muscular approach to citizenship and nationality. And no, it's not racist to say this."Babarinde introduced his PMB to the Commons using the 10-minute rule process.This gave him up to 10 minutes to make the case for why he wanted to introduce his PMB. No MP took up the option to make a 10-minute speech opposing it.Babarinde asked for his PMB, formally known as the English Ethnic Identity (census particulars) Bill, to return to the Commons on 23 April 2027 - St George's Day - for its second reading debate.But it is unlikely to be considered further in its current form due to a lack of parliamentary time.PMBs allow MPs to raise issues they believe ministers should be considering and to develop campaigns showing the strength of support for their ideas.

schema.headline: Census should include black English and Asian English options, says MP

title: Next Man Utd manager: What are club's managerial options amid doubts over Michael Carrick's future
description: Pochettino, Howe, Emery... or Carrick? Man Utd's managerial optionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe, Mauricio Pochettino and Unai E
body: Pochettino, Howe, Emery... or Carrick? Man Utd's managerial optionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Howe, Mauricio Pochettino and Unai Emery have all been linked with replacing Michael Carrick as Manchester United bossByPaul BirchBBC Sport journalistWith one victory in their first 10 Premier League matches, Manchester United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986-87 season.They are 18th in the table, one point above bottom club Crystal Palace.United directors will meet in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Michael Carrick's future as his 10-month spell as head coach comes under major scrutiny.If the 45-year-old former player departs, it would mean an eighth permanent boss for the Red Devils since Sir Alex Ferguson retired 13 years ago.That would be as many managerial changes as they have made across the previous 68 years dating back to Sir Matt Busby's appointment in 1945.BBC Sport takes a look at the leading candidates who could replace Carrick.Mauricio PochettinoImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Mauricio Pochettino penned a new deal with with the USA in the summerMajor trophies won: 1 Ligue 1, 1 French CupPremier League record: P294, W150; Win percentage: 51; Points per game ratio (PPG): 1.77Did you know: Pochettino averaged 1.89 points per game during his spell at Tottenham, the best ratio of any Spurs manager to have taken charge of 25 or more Premier League games.United's long-standing interest in the Argentine, 54, dates back a decade.At Spurs, he moulded their best team in a generation, but ultimately came up short of winning a trophy, losing both the Champions League and League Cup finals, and posted second and third-placed finishes. Silverware did come at Paris St-Germain with a league title, but a spell at Chelsea proved tougher with a League Cup final defeat by Liverpool in 2024.Having led the USA to the last 16 of the World Cup on home soil he signed a new contract taking him up to the 2030 tournament. Pochettino has an exciting group of young players to work with for the national team - led by Manchester City-bound 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan - but he has always made it clear he has unfinished business in the Premier League. A reported buyout clause in Pochettino's contract is worth $10million (£7.44m), while it is also understood to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs.Julian NagelsmannImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Julian Nagelsmann resigned in the summer after Germany lost to Paraguay on penalties in the World CupMajor trophies won: 1 BundesligaPremier League record: N/ADid you know: Only Hansi Flick (88.9%) has a better win percentage by a Bayern Munich manager in the Champions League than Nagelsmann's 83.3%.Nagelsmann first impressed with his work at Hoffenheim, where he became the youngest head coach in Bundesliga history aged 28, leading them from relegation struggles to the Champions League.He followed that by taking RB Leipzig to a Champions League semi-final in 2020 and Bayern Munich understandably came calling.But despite winning the Bundesliga title in his first season he reportedly fell out with key players and did not survive a full second season.In 2023, Nagelsmann took charge of a Germany side in transition, and they were narrowly beaten in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 by eventual winners Spain, but stepped down in the summer after Die Mannschaft were humbled by Paraguay in the World Cup last 32.Still only 39, his reputation may have taken a bit of a hit, but the German is still regarded as one of Europe's best coaches. Manchester United's director of recruitment Christopher Vivell also knows him well, having worked together at RB Leipzig.Eddie HoweImage source, BBC SportImage caption, Eddie Howe oversaw more Premier League wins (84) than any other Newcastle managerMajor trophies won: 1 League CupPremier League record: P369 W140; Win percentage: 37.9; PPG: 1.36Did you know: Eddie Howe (five) is one of only three managers with five or more wins against Mikel Arteta in all competitions, along with Pep Guardiola (11) and Jurgen Klopp (six).His body of work in English football needs little introduction having led Bournemouth to the top flight for the first time in their history, before he confirmed his place in Newcastle folklore with their first major domestic trophy since lifting the FA Cup in 1955.The League Cup final triumph over Liverpool was one of the greatest days in the club's history, while he also secured two top-five finishes to take the club back into the Champions League for the first time in 20 years.Howe, 48, left in the summer after an underwhelming 12th-placed finish last term and Newcastle would only be due a a relatively small amount of compensation should he be tempted by the Old Trafford job.Antonio ConteImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Antonio Conte called Tottenham's players "selfish" when he left after 16 months in 2023 Major trophies won: 5 Serie A, 1 Premier League, 1 FA CupPremier League record: P132, W83; Win percentage: 62.9; PPG: 2.03Did you know: Chelsea won 30 of their 38 Premier League matches as they claimed the title in Antonio Conte's first season in charge in 2016-17.A serial winner, Conte's managerial credentials are not in doubt.He left Napoli of his own accord this summer just 12 months after delivering only the fourth top-flight title in their history.That added to Serie A triumphs at Juventus (three) and Inter Milan, and spells at Chelsea and Tottenham.Conte, 57, would appear to be a no-brainer of a choice to take over at United, but could the Italian's fiery nature and history of falling out with clubs count against him?His last stint in English football ended under a cloud of controversy as he left Tottenham in 2023 following criticism of the players and the club's culture.While he had success at Chelsea, Conte also reportedly clashed with both players and the board.Unai EmeryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Emery has also managed Arsenal and Paris St-Germain in his careerMajor trophies won: 5 Europa League, 1 Ligue 1, 2 French Cups, 2 French League Cups Premier League record: P200, W101; Win percentage: 50.5; PPG: 1.75Did you know: Unai Emery has the best Premier League win percentage (51%) and points per game ratio (1.75) of any permanent Aston Villa boss.Vastly experienced, the Spaniard's stock is at an all-time high courtesy of the superb job he has done since taking over at Villa in October 2022.Having taken the club into the European Cup/Champions League for the first time for 41 years, the 55-year-old then ended their 30-year wait for silverware with success in last season's Europa League.Despite having lost the spine of his team over the summer, Emery's new-look side are finding their feet again and the chances of him leaving for United look even slimmer with recent news he is expected to sign a new contract. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Michael Carrick's Manchester United side have managed one win in 10 league games this seasonMajor trophies won: N/APremier League record: P29, W14; Win percentage: 48.3; PPG: 1.76Did you know: After his initial appointment as United's interim boss in January, Michael Carrick had the most wins (12) and points (39) of any Premier League manager during the rest of the 2025-26 season.Still clinging on to his job in the Old Trafford hot seat, could United's hierarchy actually decide to keep faith with Carrick?After such a brilliant start and end to the season following his arrival in January, the wheels have come off spectacularly this term with only three wins from 15 matches in all competitions. His team have at least shown fight with comebacks in recent games to beat Roma and salvage a point in a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, but their overall stats are damning and the outlook doesn't look good for the 45-year-old, who won five Premier League titles and the Champions League as a United player.The club are in the relegation zone and 18th is their lowest position after 10 games of a season for 40 years. It is also only the second time they have gone eight Premier League games without a victory.

schema.headline: Next Man Utd manager: What are club's managerial options amid doubts over Michael Carrick's future
